source.title: US History Ch. 21: The Civil Rights Movement, 1954–1968

concepts.name: Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can state what Brown decided and why it mattered as a starting point.
concepts.primer: The Supreme Court ruled that segregated public schools are unconstitutional, overturning Plessy's 'separate but equal'.
keyFacts: Brown held that segregated public schools are inherently unequal.
Brown overturned the 'separate but equal' doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson.
pitfalls: The ruling was resisted for years; Little Rock in 1957 showed enforcement required federal troops.

concepts.name: Montgomery bus boycott (1955–1956)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can trace the boycott from Parks's arrest to the court ruling and explain what it demonstrated.
concepts.primer: After Rosa Parks's arrest, a 381-day boycott of Montgomery's buses ended with a court ruling against bus segregation and made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader.
keyFacts: The boycott began after Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955.
The boycott lasted 381 days and ended when the courts struck down bus segregation.
pitfalls: Parks was a trained NAACP activist, and the boycott was organized within days by local leaders.

concepts.name: Little Rock Nine (1957)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain why Little Rock showed that court rulings needed federal enforcement.
concepts.primer: Nine Black students integrated Central High School only after President Eisenhower sent federal troops to enforce Brown.
keyFacts: Governor Faubus used the National Guard to block the students.
Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne to escort the students.
pitfalls: Massive resistance meant many districts stayed segregated for a decade or more.

concepts.name: Greensboro sit-ins (1960)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain how the sit-ins worked as nonviolent direct action and what organization grew from them.
concepts.primer: Four students sat at a whites-only lunch counter; the tactic spread to dozens of cities and led to SNCC.
keyFacts: Four students began the Greensboro sit-in on February 1, 1960.
The sit-ins led to the founding of SNCC.
pitfalls: Sit-ins deliberately broke segregation rules to provoke a public response; they were confrontational but disciplined.

concepts.name: Freedom Rides (1961)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can explain what the Freedom Rides tested and how violence produced federal action.
concepts.primer: Integrated groups rode interstate buses into the South to test a Supreme Court ruling; mob violence forced the federal government to enforce desegregation of terminals.
keyFacts: The riders tested a ruling that desegregated interstate bus terminals.
A bus was firebombed in Anniston, Alabama.
pitfalls: Federal action usually followed pressure and violence exposed by activists, as after Anniston.

concepts.name: Birmingham campaign (1963)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can connect the Birmingham images to the proposal of the Civil Rights Act.
concepts.primer: Televised images of police dogs and fire hoses turned on marchers, including children, shifted national opinion and pushed Kennedy to propose a civil rights bill.
keyFacts: Police under Bull Connor used dogs and fire hoses on marchers.
The images pushed Kennedy to propose a civil rights bill in June 1963.
pitfalls: Kennedy's bill followed Birmingham, the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides and years of organizing together.

concepts.name: March on Washington (1963)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can state the march's goals and its role in building support for the bill.
concepts.primer: About 250,000 people gathered for jobs and freedom; King delivered 'I Have a Dream' at the Lincoln Memorial.
keyFacts: About 250,000 people attended the march on August 28, 1963.
King delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech there.
pitfalls: It was organized by A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin around economic demands as well as civil rights.

concepts.name: Civil Rights Act of 1964
concepts.learningObjective: The student can state what the 1964 act banned and distinguish it from the 1965 act.
concepts.primer: Signed by Johnson, it outlawed segregation in public accommodations and employment discrimination.
keyFacts: Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act on July 2, 1964.
It banned segregation in public accommodations and discrimination in employment.
pitfalls: Voting protections came with the Voting Rights Act of 1965; the 1964 act targeted segregation and employment.

concepts.name: Selma and the Voting Rights Act (1965)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can connect Selma to the Voting Rights Act and state what the act did.
concepts.primer: The Bloody Sunday attack on marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge led to the Voting Rights Act, which banned literacy tests and sent federal registrars south.
keyFacts: State troopers attacked marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge on March 7, 1965.
The Voting Rights Act banned literacy tests and authorized federal registrars.
pitfalls: Selma (March 1965) came after the Civil Rights Act (July 1964); the law's date, not the chapter order, fixes the sequence.

concepts.name: Primary vs. secondary sources
concepts.learningObjective: The student can classify a document as primary or secondary from who made it, when, and why.
concepts.primer: A primary source was created by a participant or witness at the time; a secondary source interprets primary sources later.
keyFacts: A primary source is created by a participant or witness at the time.
A secondary source interprets primary sources after the fact.
pitfalls: Age doesn't decide it: a 1970 textbook about 1963 is secondary, while a 1963 photograph is primary.

concepts.name: Cause and effect in the movement
concepts.learningObjective: The student can chain at least four events of the movement from cause to consequence.
concepts.primer: Court rulings, local organizing, direct action, media coverage, and federal law fed one another in chains, not as isolated events.
keyFacts: Televised violence repeatedly turned local campaigns into national legislation.
The movement combined courts, organizing, and direct action.
pitfalls: Each event changed what was possible next: Birmingham made the 1964 act possible, Selma made the 1965 act possible.

title: The Archive of 1965

theme.setting: A shuttered newspaper archive whose vault doors only open for a researcher who can read the evidence
theme.tone: serious, investigative, warm toward the people in the story

premise: The archive's last editor sealed the story of how the movement won its laws. Rebuild the chain of events, weigh the sources, and open the final vault.

characters.name: Ida the Archivist
characters.role: keeper of the files and your guide

characters.name: The Editor
characters.role: the voice sealed in the final vault

encounters.prompt: Three file boxes describe Brown v. Board. One label is false. Which?

statements.text: The Court ruled segregated schools inherently unequal in 1954
Schools across the South desegregated within the year
statements.explanation: Resistance lasted years; Little Rock needed federal troops in 1957.

statements.text: The ruling overturned Plessy's separate but equal for schools
statements.explanation: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) had allowed segregation.

hints: A court ruling is a statement, not an enforcement.
Think about what happened at Little Rock three years later.
The false label reads: Schools across the South desegregated within the year
encounters.wrongFeedback: That box is honest. Look for the label that assumes the ruling was obeyed at once.
encounters.debriefLine: Brown v. Board: the false label was "Schools across the South desegregated within the year"; the ruling came in 1954, but enforcement took years and federal troops.

sourceRef.quote: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

encounters.targetMisconception: Rosa Parks was just a tired seamstress who acted alone.
encounters.prompt: The vault door shows the Montgomery boycott in pieces. Set the planks in order. One plank never happened.

steps: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her seat and is arrested, December 1, 1955
Local leaders organize a one-day boycott that becomes a year-long campaign
Montgomery's Black residents stay off the buses for 381 days
The Supreme Court affirms that bus segregation is unconstitutional; the boycott ends
decoys: Parks decides on the spot to start a protest movement by herself

hints: Start with the arrest and end with the court.
Between them is a year of organized walking and carpooling.
An arrest of one activist became a campaign because leaders were ready to organize.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Order matters: the boycott had to be organized before it could last 381 days, and the court ruling came at the end.
encounters.debriefLine: The Montgomery bus boycott in 4 steps: an arrest, an organized boycott, 381 days, a court ruling.

sourceRef.quote: The boycott lasted 381 days and ended after the Supreme Court affirmed that bus segregation was unconstitutional.

encounters.targetMisconception: Southern states complied with Brown once it was decided.
encounters.prompt: September 1957. Governor Faubus has posted the Arkansas National Guard to keep nine students out of Central High. What does President Eisenhower do?

params.scenario: Governor Faubus defies a federal court order by blocking nine Black students from entering Central High School with the state National Guard.

options.text: Sends the 101st Airborne to escort the students into the school
options.explanation: Eisenhower federalized the Guard and sent Army troops to enforce the court order.

options.text: Lets Arkansas decide; schools are a state matter
options.explanation: A federal court order was being defied; the president enforced it.

options.text: Cancels the desegregation order to calm the crisis
options.explanation: The order stood; the students entered under armed escort.

params.reveal: On September 25, 1957, soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division escorted the nine students into Central High School.

hints: A state governor is defying a federal court.
What tool does a president have when a court order is defied?
Think about who outranks a state's National Guard.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Brown was not self-enforcing; when a state defied a federal court, it took the president and the Army to make the ruling real.
encounters.debriefLine: Little Rock: you predicted Eisenhower's response (Sends the 101st Airborne to escort the students into the school), which showed that Brown needed federal enforcement.

sourceRef.quote: President Eisenhower responded by sending soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students into the school.

encounters.prompt: Three boxes describe the Greensboro sit-ins. One is a mimic.

statements.text: Four students sat at a whites-only lunch counter on February 1, 1960
Nonviolent meant the students avoided confrontation
statements.explanation: They deliberately broke the rules and stayed put; nonviolence was disciplined, not passive.

statements.text: The sit-ins spread to over fifty cities and led to SNCC
statements.explanation: The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee formed in April 1960.

hints: Sitting where you are forbidden to sit is itself a confrontation.
Nonviolence describes how they answered violence, not whether they provoked a response.
The mimic claims: Nonviolent meant the students avoided confrontation
encounters.wrongFeedback: That box is honest. Look for the claim that turns nonviolence into passivity.
encounters.debriefLine: Sit-ins: the mimic said "Nonviolent meant the students avoided confrontation"; nonviolent direct action broke unjust rules on purpose and answered violence with discipline.

sourceRef.quote: On February 1, 1960, four Black college students sat down at a whites-only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina.

encounters.targetMisconception: The federal government led the civil rights movement.
encounters.prompt: The dominoes of 1961 are scattered. Connect each event to what it caused.

nodes: The Supreme Court rules segregated interstate bus terminals illegal
Integrated Freedom Riders board buses to test the ruling in the Deep South
A mob firebombs a bus in Anniston, Alabama and beats the riders
Photographs of the burning bus reach national newspapers
The Kennedy administration pressures the ICC to enforce desegregated terminals
decoys: Congress passes the Civil Rights Act

hints: Start with the ruling the riders wanted to test.
Violence became news; news became pressure.
The federal enforcement came last, and not by choice.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Follow the pressure: activists tested a ruling, violence exposed the defiance, and only then did federal officials act.
encounters.debriefLine: The Freedom Rides as a causal chain: a ruling, a test, violence, headlines, then federal enforcement.

sourceRef.quote: In Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of the buses and beat the riders as they escaped.

encounters.prompt: Birmingham, spring 1963. Link each domino to the one it toppled.

nodes: The SCLC and local activists launch marches against segregation in Birmingham
Bull Connor turns police dogs and fire hoses on marchers, many of them children
Television and newspapers carry the images nationwide
Public opinion shifts and pressure on the White House mounts
President Kennedy proposes a sweeping civil rights bill in June 1963
decoys: The Voting Rights Act bans literacy tests

hints: Begin with the marches themselves.
The images only mattered because they were seen.
The bill was the last domino, not the first.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Kennedy's bill didn't come from nowhere: marches provoked violence, cameras carried it, opinion moved, then the bill followed.
encounters.debriefLine: Birmingham as cause and effect: marches, violence, images, opinion, and only then Kennedy's civil rights bill.

sourceRef.quote: The images shocked the nation, and in June 1963 President Kennedy proposed a sweeping civil rights bill.

encounters.targetMisconception: The march was only about King's speech.
encounters.prompt: Who did what at the March on Washington? Link each person to their part.

pairs.right: Veteran labor leader who first called for the march
pairs.why: He had planned a march on Washington as early as 1941.

pairs.right: Chief organizer who ran the logistics
pairs.why: He coordinated the day's transport, marshals and program.

pairs.right: Gave the closing speech remembered as I Have a Dream
pairs.why: The final speech at the Lincoln Memorial.

pairs.right: Demanded jobs and freedom, including a federal jobs program
pairs.why: The march was for Jobs and Freedom.

decoyRights: Signed the Civil Rights Act into law

hints: The march had organizers as well as a famous speaker.
Its full name was the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
The person who signed the act was a president, not a marcher.
encounters.wrongFeedback: The march was organized by labor and civil rights veterans around economic demands too; King's speech was its close, not its whole.
encounters.debriefLine: The March on Washington: you linked 4 people to their roles; it was an organized demand for jobs and freedom, not a single speech.

sourceRef.quote: On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

encounters.targetMisconception: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 guaranteed the right to vote.
encounters.prompt: Two laws, one pile of provisions. File each one under the act that created it.

bins.label: Civil Rights Act of 1964
bins.feature: attacked segregation and discrimination in public life and jobs

bins.label: Voting Rights Act of 1965
bins.feature: protected the right to register and vote

items.text: Outlawed segregation in restaurants, hotels and theaters
items.why: Public accommodations were Title II of the 1964 act.

items.text: Banned employment discrimination by race, sex, religion or national origin
Banned literacy tests for voter registration
items.why: A core provision of the 1965 act.

items.text: Sent federal registrars to counties that had blocked Black voters
items.why: Federal examiners were the 1965 act's enforcement tool.

items.text: Signed by Lyndon Johnson on July 2, 1964
items.why: The signing date of the Civil Rights Act.

items.text: Passed after the Selma marches of March 1965
items.why: Selma pushed the voting bill through Congress.

hints: Ask what each provision is about: public life and jobs, or the ballot.
Anything about registering or voting belongs to 1965.
The 1964 act's dates and titles are about accommodations and employment.
encounters.wrongFeedback: The 1964 act targeted segregation and job discrimination; voting protections waited for the 1965 act.
encounters.debriefLine: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 vs the Voting Rights Act of 1965: you filed 6 provisions by what each law protected.

sourceRef.quote: The act outlawed segregation in public accommodations such as restaurants and hotels and banned employment discrimination.

encounters.targetMisconception: Events happened in the order the textbook mentions them.
encounters.prompt: The chapter tells these out of order. Lay the planks by date. One plank belongs to a different story.

steps: President Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act, July 2, 1964
Marchers are attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, March 7, 1965
The Selma-to-Montgomery march reaches the Alabama capitol, March 25, 1965
President Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act, August 6, 1965
decoys: The Montgomery bus boycott ends, December 1956

hints: Dates decide the order, not the page they appear on.
The 1964 act came before Selma.
The voting law was signed in the summer after the march.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Use the dates: the Civil Rights Act (July 1964) came before Bloody Sunday (March 1965), and the Voting Rights Act (August 1965) came after both.
encounters.debriefLine: Selma and the Voting Rights Act in 4 dated steps: the 1964 act, Bloody Sunday, the march, the 1965 act.

sourceRef.quote: On March 7, 1965, state troopers attacked peaceful marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, a day remembered as Bloody Sunday.

encounters.prompt: Documents spill from the file cabinet. File each one as a primary or secondary source about the movement.

bins.label: Primary source
bins.feature: created by a participant or witness at the time

bins.label: Secondary source
bins.feature: created later by someone interpreting primary sources

items.text: A 1963 photograph of marchers at the Lincoln Memorial
items.why: Made at the event by a witness.

items.text: A 1971 textbook chapter on the civil rights movement
items.why: Old, but written after the fact by a non-participant.

items.text: The text of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
items.why: The document itself, from the time.

items.text: John Lewis's 1965 hospital interview about Bloody Sunday
items.why: A participant's account from the time.

hints: Ask who made it and when, not how old it is.
A textbook from 1971 is still someone else's later account.
Words or images from the people who were there are primary, even if recent.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Age doesn't decide it: a 1971 textbook about 1963 is secondary, while a 1963 photograph is primary.
encounters.debriefLine: Primary vs secondary sources: you filed 6 documents by who created them and when, not by how old they are.

sourceRef.quote: A primary source is created by a participant or witness at the time of the events, such as a letter, a photograph, or a speech.

encounters.targetMisconception: History is a list of unrelated events.
encounters.prompt: The big board. Connect the dominoes from Birmingham to the Voting Rights Act.

nodes: Televised violence in Birmingham shocks the nation, May 1963
President Kennedy proposes a civil rights bill, June 1963
President Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act, July 1964
Bloody Sunday in Selma is broadcast nationwide, March 1965
Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act, August 1965
decoys: The Supreme Court decides Brown v. Board, 1954

hints: Start in Birmingham and end with the vote.
Each law followed a televised crisis.
1963 → 1964 → 1965: two crises, two laws.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Each link is a cause and its consequence: a televised crisis produced pressure, and pressure produced a law. Brown and Montgomery matter, but they belong to an earlier chain.
encounters.debriefLine: Cause and effect in the movement: Birmingham led to Kennedy's bill and the 1964 act; Selma led to the 1965 act.

sourceRef.quote: Again and again, televised violence against nonviolent protesters turned a local campaign into national legislation.

encounters.targetMisconception: History is a list of unrelated events.
encounters.prompt: The Editor's question: why did the Voting Rights Act pass in 1965 and not before? Pin the clues, eliminate the explanations that don't fit, and name the one that stands.

params.question: Why did Congress pass the Voting Rights Act in August 1965?

hypotheses.text: Televised violence at Selma in March 1965 created national pressure that Johnson turned into a bill within days
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 had already fixed voting, so 1965 was only a technical update
It was inevitable after Brown in 1954 and needed no further events
The Supreme Court ordered Congress to pass it

clues.text: The 1964 act covered public accommodations and employment; Black registration in Selma's county was still under 2% in early 1965.
Johnson introduced the voting bill on March 15, 1965, eight days after Bloody Sunday, telling Congress 'we shall overcome'.
No court ruling in 1965 directed Congress to legislate; the bill originated in the White House.
Between 1957 and 1964 three federal laws touched voting and registration barely moved; the eleven years after Brown produced no voting act.

hints: Check each explanation against the dated clues.
What does the 2% registration figure rule out?
Only one explanation survives every clue.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Look at the clue that contradicts your pick: dated primary sources decide which explanation survives.
encounters.debriefLine: The boss: you eliminated three explanations with dated sources; the Voting Rights Act followed Selma's televised violence, which is how the movement's laws were won.

sourceRef.quote: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned literacy tests and sent federal registrars to counties that had blocked Black voters.

intro.text: Every vault in here opens for evidence, not for guesses. Read the dates. Follow the causes.

outro.text: You found the story I sealed: pressure made law, and the evidence proves it.

beats.text: The chapter's order lies. The dates don't.
Tell me why 1965. Not what happened. Why.

pre.prompt: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 do?
Which is a primary source about the 1963 March on Washington?
choices: A photograph taken at the march

post.prompt: Which of these was NOT part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
choices: Outlawing segregation in hotels and restaurants

post.prompt: A 1975 textbook chapter about the 1963 March on Washington is…
choices: A primary source, because it is about a real event
A secondary source, because it interprets events after the fact
A primary source, because it is old
The Voting Rights Act was signed
The Selma-to-Montgomery march reached the capitol
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was signed
